title: Insurance Coverage Issues for Lawyers in the Era of Generative AI
author: Mark Bassingthwaighte

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI insurance: Coverage cannot replace professional governance
st.an: Bassingthwaighte accepts that insurance is conditional and cannot displace lawyers’ professional duties, then materially develops the proposition by identifying specific coverage pathways involving the definition of professional services, intentional-act and unauthorized-practice exclusions, and cyber coverage. He consistently presents these as fact-dependent insurer arguments rather than settled outcomes.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source accepts that generative AI offers practical benefits but requires active risk assessment during deployment. It materially extends the cluster’s governance framework by adding professional-liability insurance analysis, including the possibility that AI-related negligence may fall outside coverage depending on the policy’s definition of professional services.

I suspect it’s because of what I do for a living, but as I see it, in order to fully understand the associated risks of deploying generative AI, one mustn’t forget to look into the associated insurance coverage implications.

st.an: The source does not quantify AI-malpractice incidence, but materially develops the synthesis’s coverage analysis. It treats noncoverage as conditional rather than established, identifying professional-services definitions, intentional-act exclusions and unauthorized-practice exclusions as possible insurer arguments, while reinforcing verification and lawyer supervision as practical controls.

kp.k: Generative AI adoption is rapid and expanding
kp.d: Writing in 2025, Bassingthwaighte asserts that lawyers across firms of all shapes and sizes are already finding increasingly creative uses for generative AI. He presents the technology as offering substantial, still-developing opportunities to enhance legal-service delivery, while stressing lawyers’ ethical obligation to understand the associated risks.
qs: However, one thing I did get right was realizing how significant generative AI would become, how fast its adoption would be, and how much of its potential yet remains to be developed.
When it comes to generative AI the future is here and lawyers in firms of every shape and size are finding ever more creative ways to tap into its potential.
Of course, as with all things tech related, lawyers also have an ethical obligation to explore and understand the associated risks of any tech deployed in a law practice.

kp.k: AI-related negligence may fall outside malpractice coverage
kp.d: The author reports that lawyers’ professional liability policies generally did not exclude generative-AI negligence claims at the time of writing, but cautions that coverage may turn on whether the conduct qualifies as “professional services.” An insurer could argue that blindly relying on fabricated, incorrect or misleading AI output involved no professional service and possibly invoke an intentional-act exclusion.
qs: At the time of this writing, lawyers’ professional liability (LPL) policies typically do not exclude coverage for claims alleging negligence arising as a result of the use of generative AI.
That said, coverage may depend on whether the conduct at issue meets the policy’s definition of “professional services.”

If this lawyer is unable to demonstrate that she exercised reasonable care and due diligence with her use of the AI tool, then an insurer could argue that no professional service was ever provided because the lawyer simply chose to blindly rely on third-party technology.
If the subject lawyer did make a deliberate decision to blindly accept the output as accurate, this act might also trigger a policy’s intentional act exclusion.

kp.k: Lawyers must verify and own AI output
kp.d: Bassingthwaighte recommends verification of all AI-generated output and maintains that professional competence, diligence, accountability and responsibility cannot be delegated to technology. This human-review requirement is presented both as risk management and as a continuing professional duty.
qs: A risk management takeaway is lawyers must always accept accountability and responsibility for all AI-generated output by validating the accuracy of outputs.
Understand that a lawyer’s duties of competence and diligence can never be delegated to a machine.
It’s as simple as that.

kp.k: Public-facing AI creates coverage and UPL risks
kp.d: The author argues that chatbots, DIY form generators and other public- or client-facing AI services may generate uncovered malpractice claims when systems make critical legal judgments without lawyer oversight. Depending on the circumstances and jurisdiction, this may be treated as unauthorized practice of law or as a situation in which no attorney rendered professional services.
qs: If a law firm markets AI-generated content or tools (e.g., an online chatbot or a DIY legal form generator) directly to clients or the public and a malpractice claim arose out of that service, would this be a covered claim?

First, if firm lawyers allowed the AI to make critical legal judgements without attorney oversight, this could be viewed as the unauthorized practice of law, and LPL policies typically exclude coverage for the unauthorized practice of law.
Second, the lack of attorney oversight also implies that no professional services were rendered by an attorney; and as you now know, no professional service means no coverage.
In short, over-reliance on an AI tool, or allowing it to make legal decisions without attorney oversight can create unintended consequences.

kp.k: AI remains subject to lawyer supervision and review
kp.d: For AI systems interacting with clients or the public, the author recommends caution and continuous attorney supervision. He analogizes AI to a non-human staff member and argues that its non-human status does not reduce lawyers’ responsibility to review its work.
qs: A risk management takeaway is to exercise caution when deploying AI tools that interact directly with the public and/or clients because a lawyer’s duty to supervise and review all work remains paramount.
The fact that an AI Tool is a non-human member of the “staff” makes not one iota of a difference.

kp.k: Confidential AI inputs can create uninsured data risks
kp.d: The author warns that entering sensitive or confidential client information into public, cloud-based or insufficiently secured generative-AI systems could cause unauthorized access or a data breach. He states that malpractice coverage may be unavailable because of confidentiality or intentional-act exclusions, although cyber liability insurance may cover some incidents depending on their specific circumstances.
qs: Feeding sensitive or confidential client information into a generative AI tool, especially one that is cloud-based and accessible to the public or not specifically designed for secure use by legal professionals, could result in a data breach or unauthorized access to this client information potentially giving rise to a claim.
The reason is that most LPL policies have exclusions related to intentional acts or breaches of confidentiality that are not the result of a negligent act.
That said, if your firm has purchased cyber liability insurance, coverage may be available under that policy depending upon the specific circumstances of any breach.
Just be aware that here too an intentional acts exclusion could come into play.

kp.k: Secure platforms and terms review reduce confidentiality exposure
kp.d: As risk management, Bassingthwaighte recommends using AI platforms with firm data-privacy assurances, data-retention opt-outs and compliance with applicable data-protection regulations. He also says lawyers must read and understand each platform’s terms of service before use.
qs: A risk management takeaway is to only use generative AI platforms that come with strict data privacy assurances, allow users to opt out from data retention, and are in compliance with your jurisdiction’s data protection regulations.
And yes, this does mean you need to read and understand the terms of service before using any generative AI platform.

kp.k: AI opportunities depend on managing insurance coverage risks
kp.d: The article’s overall position is that generative AI can improve how legal services are delivered, but lawyers should include insurance implications in deployment decisions. The three highlighted concerns—AI-output malpractice, unsupervised public-facing tools and confidentiality or security failures—are presented as important but not exhaustive.
qs: Thus, the following are a few key considerations lawyers should keep in mind when integrating generative AI into their practice.

I hope this information helps you in any generative AI decision-making process going forward because I do believe that generative AI offers incredible opportunities for our profession, opportunities that will enhance how legal services are delivered.
While these three coverage concerns aren’t the only concerns with AI, they are ones I believe every lawyer should be most aware of.

pts.k: Bassingthwaighte describes rapid, broad adoption of generative AI and anticipates further improvements in legal-service delivery.
pts.d: Mark Bassingthwaighte, ALPS Insurance risk manager, states that firms of all sizes are finding new uses for generative AI and that substantial potential remains undeveloped. His expectation that AI will enhance legal services is general: he specifies neither measurable improvements nor a timetable.

pts.k: Reliance on inaccurate AI output can produce negligence claims and potentially leave lawyers without professional liability coverage.
pts.d: Bassingthwaighte says lawyers’ professional liability policies typically do not expressly exclude generative-AI negligence claims. Nevertheless, he argues that an insurer could deny coverage if blind reliance on AI fails to qualify as professional services, or that a deliberate decision to accept output without checking might trigger an intentional-act exclusion. He presents these as possible coverage outcomes, not established rulings. Human verification and continuing lawyer accountability are his prescribed safeguards.

pts.k: Client-facing or public-facing AI without lawyer oversight can introduce unauthorized-practice and insurance-coverage risks.
pts.d: Bassingthwaighte discusses firms marketing AI-generated content, chatbots or DIY legal form generators directly to clients or the public. He argues that allowing AI to make critical legal judgments without attorney oversight could be treated as unauthorized practice of law, which he says LPL policies typically exclude. Separately, the absence of attorney oversight could mean no covered professional service was rendered. His distinction is between supervised AI use and AI making legal decisions without oversight, rather than a claim that every client-facing tool is excluded.

pts.k: Entering confidential client information into AI systems can create data-security claims that malpractice insurance may not cover; cyber coverage is also conditional.
pts.d: Bassingthwaighte identifies heightened risks from publicly accessible cloud-based tools or tools not designed for secure legal use. He states that disclosure can lead to a breach or unauthorized access, potentially generating a claim. He attributes possible LPL noncoverage to intentional-act exclusions or exclusions for confidentiality breaches not resulting from negligence. Purchased cyber liability insurance may provide coverage, but circumstances and intentional-act exclusions still matter. He recommends privacy assurances, retention opt-outs, regulatory compliance and review of platform terms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source offers professional risk-management judgment and generalized descriptions of insurance terms, rather than empirical findings or documented coverage decisions.
pts.d: Bassingthwaighte writes in his capacity as a risk manager. His analysis relies on hypothetical negligence, unsupervised legal advice and confidentiality scenarios, together with assertions about typical policy definitions and exclusions and lawyers’ continuing ethical duties. The document supplies no adoption data, benchmarks, specific policy text, cited legal authority, named claims, court decisions or insurer determinations substantiating these outcomes. Its broad benefits forecast is expressly framed as personal belief.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Coverage claims concern conditions at publication on August 21, 2025; future benefits have no specified horizon.
pts.d: The author qualifies the description of typical LPL coverage as current at writing. Potential noncoverage depends on policy wording, whether conduct counts as professional services, reasonable care and due diligence, deliberate unchecked reliance, attorney oversight, the jurisdiction and circumstances, and the nature of a confidentiality breach. Cyber coverage additionally requires that the firm purchased such insurance. The article does not predict when policy practices might change or when further AI benefits will materialize.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims concern lawyers and firms of all sizes, their clients, users of public-facing legal tools, and their insurers.
pts.d: Lawyers and firms gain potential service-delivery benefits while retaining verification, supervision, competence, diligence and confidentiality responsibilities and facing possible uninsured claims. Clients can be exposed to inaccurate legal outputs or compromised confidential information; members of the public can encounter unsupervised firm-provided AI tools. LPL and cyber insurers are implicated through the policy definitions and exclusions the author identifies. The source does not differentiate effects by firm size, practice area or client market, and does not make a specific access-to-justice, employment or pricing prediction.
